property_summary: For any caller and any nonnegative ETH value sent, calling addToBalance can never decrease that caller's stored userBalance (i.e., userBalance after the call >= before); the mutant that subtracts msg.value breaks this by making the balance decrease for some inputs.

For any caller and any nonnegative ETH value sent, calling addToBalance never decreases ANY account's stored userBalance (every user's balance after the call is >= before); the mutant that subtracts msg.value can make some account's balance decrease.

For any caller A and any nonnegative payment v, calling addToBalance() increases A's recorded balance by exactly v (i.e., newBalance == oldBalance + v); the mutant that subtracts msg.value causes newBalance < oldBalance + v for some inputs.
After calling addToBalance twice with amounts a>0 and b>0, the stored balance equals a+b (i.e., balances accumulate rather than being overwritten).
After calling addToBalance twice from this contract, the stored balance for this contract equals the sum of the two deposited amounts.
After depositing two positive amounts a and b by calling addToBalance twice from this contract, the stored balance for this contract equals a + b.
After calling addToBalance twice from this contract with positive amounts a and b, the stored balance for this contract equals a + b.
After calling addToBalance twice from this contract with positive amounts a and b, the stored balance for this contract equals a + b.

After any call to addToBalance() by an actor sending value v, the contract's stored balance for that actor is at least v (i.e., addToBalance adds the sent value to the existing balance, so userBalance[actor] >= msg.value); the mutant that overwrites the balance with msg.value can make userBalance for other actors decrease relative to the reference and thus violate this monotonicity for some inputs.

For any caller and any value, after a successful addToBalance() the caller's recorded userBalance equals the amount they previously had plus msg.value (i.e., addToBalance always increases only the caller's balance by msg.value); the buggy modifier can allow reentrancy during the external call path and may let an attacker alter balances of other users, violating this invariant for some inputs.

For every addToBalance call that completes, C preserves all other users' balances (only the caller's balance increases by msg.value); the mutated modifier can enable reentrant calls that alter other users' balances during addToBalance, violating this rule for some inputs.

For every addToBalance call that completes, the contract's total Ether held (address(c).balance) equals the sum of all userBalance entries (so addToBalance never lets Ether leave or be double-counted); the buggy modifier can enable reentrancy that withdraws or misattributes Ether during addToBalance, breaking that equality for some inputs.

For any caller and any deposit amount, after a completed addToBalance call, no other user's balance may increase as a result of that call; the buggy modifier enabling reentrancy can let an attacker re-enter during addToBalance and increase another user's balance, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller and any deposited amount, after addToBalance completes the caller's userBalance equals the previous balance plus msg.value (i.e., addToBalance atomically credits exactly the caller's own balance) — the buggy modifier allows reentrancy during the deposit which can cause the caller's recorded balance to differ from previous + msg.value for some inputs (attacker contract and ordering).

After any successful addToBalance call by any actor with any amount, the reference contract preserves that no other account's balance decreases as a result (i.e., total userBalance of every address never decreases due to addToBalance), whereas removing the require guard allows a re-entrant attacker to withdraw another user's balance during addToBalance causing some address's stored balance to decrease.

After any call to addToBalance by any actor sending any amount, the caller's stored userBalance in the reference increases by exactly the sent amount (no reentrant interference can change the caller's own recorded balance during its addToBalance), whereas removing the reentrancy require allows a reentrant attacker to manipulate the caller's recorded balance so this equality can fail.

For every actor and amount, after a successful addToBalance call the caller's recorded userBalance is at least the previous balance plus the sent amount (the reference prevents reentrant withdrawals that could reduce balances), whereas removing the require allows a reentrant attacker to withdraw and make that inequality fail for some inputs.

For any attacker address A and deposit amount v, if A calls addToBalance sending v, then immediately after the call completes the total contract Ether balance equals the sum of all userBalance entries (i.e., address(c).balance == sum_over_some_addresses userBalance[address]); the missing require allows reentrant withdrawals that can make contract ETH balance not match recorded userBalance sums.

For any attacker address A and victim V and deposit amount v, if V calls addToBalance sending v while A is a malicious contract that reenters on receiving funds, then in the correct contract V's stored balance for V after the call is exactly previousBalance(V) + v (the nonReentrant guard prevents other accounts from draining V during V's add), but the mutant (missing require) can let A reenter during V's add and cause V's stored balance to be less than previousBalance(V) + v for some inputs.
For any address u, getBalance(u) must return the stored userBalance for that address; the mutant instead returns the caller's balance, so when caller != u the mutant can return a different value.

After a successful addToBalance call by any user, that user's recorded balance in C equals the sum of their previous balance and the value sent; removing the reentrancy guard allows an attacker to reenter during addToBalance and make the final recorded balance differ (the mutant can be exploited to change observed balance).

After a call to addToBalance by any caller sending value V, the caller's recorded balance (getBalance) increases by exactly V in the correct contract for all inputs; removing the nonReentrant_ guard permits a reentrant attacker to manipulate the final recorded balance so this invariant can be violated for some inputs.

For any caller and any Ether amount, after addToBalance completes in the correct contract, the contract's recorded balance for that caller equals the contract's stored userBalance for that caller (i.e., address(c).balance >= sum of all userBalance entries and specifically the caller's getBalance increased by the sent amount without being reduced by a reentrant attack) — removing the nonReentrant_ guard allows a reentrant attacker to reenter during addToBalance and alter the final stored userBalance so this relation can be broken for some inputs.

For any caller and any nonzero ether amount, when a caller calls addToBalance on the correct contract C the final stored userBalance for that caller equals the amount they sent (no reentrant calls can alter it during addToBalance); removing the nonReentrant_ guard allows a malicious payable contract to reenter during addToBalance and make the final stored balance differ for some fuzzed (caller, amount).

For any caller A and amount V, if A is a contract that reenters during its receive() when addToBalance sends value (i.e., a reentrant attacker), the reference C's nonReentrant_ modifier prevents reentry so after addToBalance completes A's recorded balance equals V (previous zero) — removing the guard allows the attacker to reenter and cause the final stored balance to be > V for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller and any deposited amount, calling withdrawBalance always results in the caller's recorded userBalance being zero afterwards (reference preserves clearing after successful external transfer), whereas the mutant that zeroes the balance before sending can cause the contract to send zero value and thus leave the caller's funds effectively not transferred (observable as address(c).balance remaining larger) or change behavior when the external call fails — the reference always attempts to transfer the stored balance and then clears it, but the mutant transfers zero and leaves funds in the contract.
After a successful withdrawBalance call, the caller's recorded userBalance must be zero (reference C always zeros the balance; the mutant that removes the zeroing can leave a non-zero balance).

For any depositor and deposit amount > 0, after calling withdrawBalance the reference contract always leaves the contract's ETH balance reduced by the withdrawn amount (i.e., address(c).balance decreases by the depositor's prior credited amount), but the mutant that fails to zero the user's balance can be exploited (via a reentrant attacker) to withdraw more than the contract's balance change would indicate — the missing zeroing lets an attacker reenter and drain extra funds so the invariant on address(c).balance change is violated.

After a user deposits funds, calling withdrawBalance() will always set that user's balance to 0 in the correct contract; removing the lock allows a reentrant attacker to cause withdrawBalance to complete while the victim's balance is not zeroed (or drained multiple times), violating that invariant for some inputs.

For any depositor and any deposit amount, after calling withdrawBalance() the contract's balance for that depositor is zero in the correct contract; removing the reentrancy lock allows a reentrant attacker to cause withdrawBalance to complete while the depositor's stored balance is nonzero for some inputs (attacker triggers reentry during external call).

For any depositor and any deposit amount, when withdrawBalance() is called by that depositor through an adversarial reentrant counterparty, the reference contract ensures the depositor's recorded userBalance becomes zero after withdrawBalance() completes; the mutant that removes the locking allows a reentrant attacker to reenter and corrupt the final stored balance so this can remain nonzero.

For any depositor address and any nonzero deposit amount, if that depositor funds the contract then calls withdrawBalance (possibly via a helper address that forwards the call), the reference contract ensures the depositor's userBalance is zero after withdrawBalance finishes; the mutant that removes the reentrancy locking allows a malicious recipient (an attacker contract used as msg.sender) to reenter during the external call and make the depositor's stored balance remain nonzero for some inputs, violating this rule.

For any attacker deposit amount and attacker address, if the attacker who has a positive balance calls withdrawBalance(), then after withdrawBalance() returns the contract's ETH balance must be 0 (all funds withdrawn) in the reference; the mutant lacking the reentrancy lock can be reentered to withdraw multiple times leaving contract balance nonzero for some fuzzed amounts/addresses.

Invariant: after any caller deposits X and then calls withdrawBalance, the caller's userBalance is 0 in the correct contract (withdraw sends the stored balance); the mutant that zeroes before sending can leave other accounts' balances unchanged or allow a reentrant attacker to obtain funds and cause a differing stored balance for some key, so there exists an input (attacker account depositing then withdrawing via a reentrant helper) that makes balances diverge.
